statement: Levenberg–Marquardt damping is the modification of the Gauss–Newton normal equations by adding a non-negative damping term proportional to the identity matrix or to the diagonal of the Hessian approximation, yielding the damped linear system (\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J} + \lambda \mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}[\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{f}(\boldsymbol{\beta})] or [\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J} + \lambda \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J})]\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}[\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{f}(\boldsymbol{\beta})], where \lambda \ge 0$ is the damping factor determining the increment \boldsymbol{\delta}$ to the parameter vector \boldsymbol{\beta}.

symbols.meaning: parameter vector of the model curve
increment/step vector to the estimated parameter vector
vector of dependent variable observations y_i
Jacobian matrix with i-th row \mathbf{J}_i = \partial f(x_i, \boldsymbol{\beta}) / \partial \boldsymbol{\beta}
non-negative damping factor adjusted at each iteration
diagonal matrix containing the diagonal elements of \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J}

properties.property: Interpolation between Gauss–Newton and gradient descent
properties.why: A small \lambda brings the step closer to Gauss–Newton, while a large \lambda directs the step opposite to the gradient -2(\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}[\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{f}(\boldsymbol{\beta})])^{\mathrm{T}}

When \lambda is large relative to \|\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J}\|, the update is well-approximated by \lambda^{-1}\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}[\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{f}(\boldsymbol{\beta})] without matrix inversion
Replacing \mathbf{I} with \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J}) scales each gradient component according to curvature, avoiding slow convergence in directions of small gradient
The parameter \lambda is reduced when residual sum of squares decreases rapidly and increased when an iteration gives insufficient residual reduction

properties.property: Equivalence to Tikhonov regularization and ridge regression
properties.why: A mathematically identical damping factor appears in Tikhonov regularization for linear ill-posed problems and ridge regression in statistics

assumptions.breaks_when: \lambda is negative, which can destroy positive semi-definiteness and cause \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{J} + \lambda \mathbf{I} to become singular or indefinite

assumptions.assumption: The model function f(x_i, \boldsymbol{\beta}) is differentiable with respect to the parameter vector \boldsymbol{\beta}
assumptions.breaks_when: f is non-differentiable or the partial derivatives \mathbf{J}_i do not exist

assumptions.assumption: An initial parameter guess \boldsymbol{\beta} is provided that is sufficiently close to the global minimum in multi-minima problems
assumptions.breaks_when: The objective function possesses multiple local minima and the initial guess is far from the global minimum

failure_modes.signature: Optimization terminates at a suboptimal parameter estimate with high residual sum of squares
failure_modes.cause: Presence of multiple minima combined with an initial guess located outside the basin of attraction of the global minimum

failure_modes.mode: Slow convergence near the optimum under steepest descent regime
failure_modes.signature: Very small residual reductions per iteration despite being near the optimum
failure_modes.cause: Heuristic damping factor selection excessively increases \lambda, causing the method to suffer from slow convergence characteristic of steepest descent

failure_modes.signature: Iteration stops before reaching the minimum because step length \|\boldsymbol{\delta}\| or reduction in sum of squares falls below predefined thresholds
failure_modes.cause: Successive unsuccessful uphill steps cause repeated multiplications of \lambda, shrinking the step size \boldsymbol{\delta} below numerical tolerance
